title: Addiction and the Long Road Back
subtitle: The enslaved will without the easy moralism. What addiction actually is, why willpower alone has never freed anyone, where the gospel of grace meets the Twelve Steps, and the long, crooked, possible road of recovery for the body and the soul together.

connections.label: The Anxious Mind: Faith and Mental Health
Suffering and the Silence of God

parts.title: The Promise You Have Broken to Yourself
parts.body:
You meant it when you said never again. You meant it the last time, and the time before that, with everything in you, and then it happened again anyway, and that is the part that is breaking you, not only the thing itself but what the thing has revealed, that your own will, the thing you thought was you, cannot be trusted to do what you have decided with your whole heart to do. You are not weak in the way people think. You have wanted to stop more desperately than anyone watching could imagine. And you could not, and the gap between what you want and what you do has become a kind of horror.

Maybe it is alcohol, the bottle you swore you had under control until the morning you understood you did not. Maybe it is opioids, which arrived as a prescription and stayed as a master. Maybe it is pornography, the secret that has colonized your marriage and your sense of yourself. Maybe it is gambling, or food, or the pills, or the screen, or the next thing that promised relief and delivered a chain. Addiction does not care about your respectability. It is in the pews and the pulpits, in the suburbs and the recovery houses, and it wears a different face on every person it has hold of, but underneath it is the same thing, a will that has been taken captive by the very thing it reaches for to feel free.

And then there is what the church often did, which was to treat it as a simple matter of sin and willpower, to tell you to repent and pray and try harder, as if you had not been trying harder for years, as if the problem were that you had not yet been shamed enough to stop. The moralism cut deep, because you knew there was real sin tangled in it and you also knew that try harder had never once worked, and the church seemed to have only the one tool. So you learned to hide it, to perform sobriety on Sunday and relapse on Tuesday, and to tell no one, because telling someone in that room felt like signing your own exile.

Let me say the thing the moralism missed and the gospel has always known. Addiction is the enslaved will, and an enslaved will cannot free itself by deciding to. That is not an excuse. It is a diagnosis, and it happens to be the exact diagnosis the apostle Paul gave of the whole human condition, the good that I want to do I do not do, but the evil I do not want to do, this I keep on doing. The honest place to begin is not with more willpower. It is with the end of the illusion that willpower was ever going to be enough, because that end is, strangely, the doorway to the only freedom that has ever actually worked. You cannot save yourself. That is not the bad news. In the gospel and in the recovery rooms alike, it turns out to be where the road back begins.

parts.title: What Addiction Costs and Why the Church Must Understand It
parts.body:
It matters because addiction is killing people, in numbers that should stop us cold. The overdose deaths alone in recent years have run past a hundred thousand a year in the United States, and behind each number is a family, a congregation, a person who was someone's child. This is not a marginal pastoral concern. It is one of the defining crises of the age, and the people dying are not strangers to the church. They are in the church, or were, until the shame or the relapse or the silence pushed them out. A faith that cannot meet the addict is a faith that is missing in action at one of the great catastrophes of our time.

It matters because addiction destroys far more than the addict. It hollows out marriages, terrorizes children, drains savings, and teaches a whole family to organize itself around the unpredictable storm at its center. The spouse becomes a manager of crises, the children become small adults who learned too early not to trust the ground, and the wreckage radiates outward for a generation. To care about addiction is to care about everyone in the blast radius, which is to say it is to care about a very large part of any community honestly examined.

It matters because how the church handles addiction reveals whether it has understood its own gospel. We are a community founded on the confession that none of us can save ourselves, that we are all of us captive to sin and freed only by grace we did not earn, and yet we have often handed the addict the one message the gospel most explicitly denies, that the answer is to try harder and clean yourself up. The recovery movement, in a strange providence, has frequently preached the gospel's own logic of grace and surrender more clearly than the churches that gave it birth, and that should humble us. I have, in earlier years, offered an addict a sermon when he needed a meeting, a doctor, and a community that would not flinch, and I called my inadequacy faithfulness.

And it matters because the addict, sitting in the back of the room convinced he is beyond help, is exactly the person Jesus came for, and the watching world is watching to see whether we believe that. When the church learns to receive the addict not as a project or a scandal but as a fellow captive being freed by the same grace, something becomes visible that no sermon on grace could convey. A people who actually believe that nobody saves himself, and who treat the most enslaved among them as living proof that grace is real.

parts.title: What Scripture Sees in the Enslaved Will
parts.body:
Scripture understood addiction long before we had the word, because Scripture understood the enslaved will, which is the thing underneath every addiction. Paul writes the definitive account in Romans 7, and it reads like a transcript from a recovery meeting. I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing. And then the cry that every addict has prayed, wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death. Paul is not describing a character flaw. He is describing the bondage of the will, the terrible truth that wanting to stop and being able to stop are two different things, and that the gap between them is where a person can drown.

Notice that Scripture refuses both of the cheap answers the world hands the addict. It refuses the moralism that says you could stop if you really wanted to, because Paul himself, the apostle, says he could not simply will his way out of his own bondage. And it refuses the determinism that says you are nothing but your chemistry and your conditioning, helpless and unaccountable, because Paul never stops calling the captivity a real captivity from which a real deliverance is needed and possible. The biblical picture is harder and more hopeful than either, a will that is genuinely enslaved and genuinely able to be freed, not by trying harder but by being rescued from outside.

And the rescue is the whole point. Paul does not end Romans 7 in the wretchedness. He turns, and the turn is everything. Who will deliver me from this body of death. Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. The answer to the enslaved will is not a better technique of self-mastery. It is a deliverer, a power from outside the self, breaking in to free what the self could not free. This is the gospel's deepest logic, and it is also, remarkably, the logic the recovery movement stumbled into, that the first step toward freedom is admitting you are powerless, and the second is believing that a Power greater than yourself can restore you. The addict who finally stops trying to save himself and turns to the One who can save him is not failing at the Christian life. He is doing the most Christian thing there is.

And Scripture never treats the person as a soul detached from a body, which matters enormously here, because addiction is in the body. When Elijah collapsed in despair, God did not rebuke him. He fed him and let him sleep, tending the body before addressing the soul, because a person is not a spirit carried around by an inconvenient body but a whole creature, body and soul together. The God who made the body and called it good is not offended by the doctor, the medication, the treatment program, the slow physical work of a nervous system relearning how to live without the substance. He is the author of healing through means. The gospel that frees the will and the medicine that heals the body are not rivals. They are two hands of the same God, who came to set the captives free, body and soul, and who is patient enough for the long, crooked road that real freedom takes.

parts.title: The Church, the Steps, and the Long Wisdom of the Captive Will
parts.body:
The church has known about enslaving habits for a very long time, even when it lacked the modern vocabulary. The desert fathers and mothers of the fourth century built a whole practical psychology around the passions, the disordered desires that take hold of a person and drive them, and they understood that these could not simply be willed away. Evagrius of Pontus catalogued the patterns by which a thought becomes a craving and a craving becomes a master, and the counsel of the desert was strikingly modern, that you do not defeat the passion by sheer force of will but by vigilance, by community, by replacing the disordered love with an ordered one, by the slow retraining of the heart under grace. They knew, fifteen centuries before the recovery rooms, that the captive will is freed gradually and never alone.

Augustine wrote the first great account of addiction from the inside, in the Confessions, around the year 397. He describes his own bondage with unforgettable honesty, a will divided against itself, commanding itself and not obeyed, wanting to be free of his lusts and unable to break them, and he names the mechanism precisely, that habit untreated becomes necessity, that the chain is forged of his own repeated choices until he can no longer simply choose otherwise. And he describes the only thing that finally broke it, not a redoubled effort of will but grace, a deliverance that came from outside him when his own resources were exhausted. Augustine is the patron saint of everyone who has ever been unable to stop, and his answer is the gospel's answer, that the divided will is healed not by the will but by grace.

The modern recovery movement carries this ancient wisdom in a form the church should recognize as its own child. Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in 1935 by Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith, and its roots run directly back through the Oxford Group, a Christian movement, to the gospel itself. The Twelve Steps are, in their bones, a translation of Christian conversion into the language of the recovery room. Admit you are powerless. Believe a Power greater than yourself can restore you. Turn your will and your life over to God as you understand him. Make a searching moral inventory. Confess your wrongs. Make amends. Carry the message to others. Read those next to the gospel and the parallels are not accidental. The movement recovered, for millions whom the church had failed, the gospel's own logic of surrender, confession, restitution, community, and dependence on a higher power, and it did so with a humility about human self-sufficiency that the moralizing church had often lost.

And the church has, at its best, kept producing the wisdom of the captive will, in the care of souls that knew sin was bondage and not merely choice, in the pastors who understood that you do not free a slave by scolding him, in the temperance movements that, whatever their excesses, took seriously the wreckage that addiction leaves. The recovery now happening, where churches partner with treatment, where congregations host meetings in their basements, where believers in recovery testify openly to a freedom they did not manufacture, is not a borrowing from a secular movement. It is the church recognizing its own oldest insight come home, that no one saves himself, that the captive is freed by grace working through community and means, and that the road back is long, and possible, and walked together.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Addiction has been studied intensely by neuroscientists, physicians, and psychologists, and the believer can learn from all of it without fear. All truth is God's truth, and honest research into the captive will has often confirmed what Scripture and the desert fathers already knew. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each gets right, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of addiction carries a hidden picture of what a human being is and what freedom means, and the picture is where the matter is decided.

secular.source: The disease model and the neuroscience of addiction
secular.author: Nora Volkow and addiction medicine
secular.whatItGetsRight: The brain research has established beyond serious dispute that addiction physically rewires the reward system, hijacking the circuits meant for survival so that the substance comes to feel as necessary as food, and that this rewiring outlasts the substance and drives relapse long after a person has decided to stop. This is a needed demolition of the lazy moralism that treats addiction as a simple failure of character. The craving is real, it is physical, and willpower alone has never been a match for a rewired brain.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture agrees the bondage is real and reaches into the body, that a person is dust and breath together and that the flesh wars against the will. The disease model rightly removes the shame of treating addiction as mere weakness. Where it must be tested is in the conclusion some draw, that the addict is therefore only a malfunctioning brain with no moral agency at all. Scripture holds both at once, a will genuinely enslaved and a person genuinely responsible, captive and yet called, sick and yet summoned. Disease is part of the story. It is not the whole person, who is also a moral agent in need of forgiveness and capable, by grace, of being freed.

secular.source: Alcoholics Anonymous and the Twelve Step movement
secular.author: Bill Wilson and the recovery tradition
secular.whatItGetsRight: The Twelve Step movement has freed more addicts than any program in history, and it did so by recovering truths the moralizing culture had lost, that the first step is admitting powerlessness, that surrender to a higher power is the doorway rather than the defeat, that confession and amends and rigorous honesty are essential, and that recovery happens in community, one day at a time, carried by people walking the same road. Few human movements have so closely mirrored the gospel's own shape.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The parallels to Scripture are profound, and there is one place the believer must press. The Steps speak of a higher power as you understand him, a deliberate vagueness that opens the door to many while leaving the deliverer undefined. Scripture rejoices in the powerlessness and the surrender and then names the Power, the living God revealed in Jesus Christ, who is not a useful concept but a person who actually died and rose to break the chains. The recovery rooms have the right shape and an open center. The gospel fills the center with a specific Savior, which means the believer can embrace the Steps gratefully while knowing the higher power has a name, and a face, and scars.

secular.author: Modern addiction medicine
secular.whatItGetsRight: The evidence is overwhelming that for opioid addiction in particular, medication-assisted treatment dramatically reduces overdose deaths and supports lasting recovery, that medications like buprenorphine and methadone are not a substitution of one addiction for another but a medical stabilization that makes recovery possible. This is a gift of common grace, like insulin for the diabetic, and the stigma against it within some recovery circles and some churches has cost lives that did not have to be lost.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture insists that a person is body and soul together and that God heals through means, through farmers and physicians and medicine, which means there is no faithfulness in refusing a treatment that keeps a person alive. The temptation to test here is the reductive one, that the medication is the whole answer and the soul can be ignored, just stabilize the chemistry and the person is fixed. Just take the medicine ignores the soul, as just have faith ignores the body. The faithful path takes the medication seriously, gratefully, as the floor under a recovery that also reaches the heart, the relationships, and the God who is the deepest healing of all.

secular.source: In the Realm of Hungry Ghosts and the trauma model of addiction
secular.author: Gabor Mate
secular.whatItGetsRight: Mate argues with great compassion that addiction is very often rooted in trauma and pain, that the substance is reached for as relief from an unbearable inner wound, and that the right question is not why the addiction but why the pain. This is a profound corrective to the punitive approach, and it reaches a truth the church should already know, that people in bondage are usually people who are suffering, and that contempt has never healed anyone.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture deeply affirms the compassion here, that the captive is usually also the wounded, and that the right posture toward the addict is the tenderness of the One who will not break a bruised reed. Mate sees the pain underneath the addiction clearly. Where his account stops is at the moral and the eternal. A human being is more than the sum of their wounds, also a moral agent who needs forgiveness and a creature made for God whose deepest hunger no relief from pain can finally fill. Augustine named the real hungry ghost, the restless heart that finds no rest until it rests in God. The trauma is real and must be tended. It is not the bottom of the matter.

secular.source: Habit science and the architecture of craving
secular.author: Charles Duhigg and the study of habit
secular.whatItGetsRight: The research on habit loops has illuminated the mechanics of how a craving works, the cue, the routine, the reward, and how environment and trigger drive behavior far more than conscious choice, which is why changing the surroundings and the patterns matters as much as resolving to do better. This confirms the practical wisdom that recovery is built by changing the architecture of a life, not merely by gritting one's teeth, and it gives the struggling person concrete handles where moralism gave only shame.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture has always known that human beings are formed by repetition, which is why it gives practices, the table, the day of rest, the gathered community, the daily prayer, and why the recovery rooms insist on the daily meeting and the changed routine. Habit science is a true account of the how and silent on the what and the why. It can teach you to rearrange your triggers and cannot give you a new heart, nor reckon with the deeper truth that the craving underneath the craving is for God. The science is a real servant of recovery. It is not the master, because the will it helps to retrain is itself in need of a rescue no rearranged environment can supply.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Bible and the same love for the addict still differ on how to understand addiction and how recovery best happens. The difference is serious and it shapes how people are treated, and it is not the difference between those who take sin seriously and those who do not. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are honoring something true, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Addiction is fundamentally a sin to be repented of and put to death
views.body: This view begins with the conviction that addiction, whatever its physical dimensions, is at its root a disorder of worship, a created desire bent toward a false god, and that the deepest help comes from naming it as sin and bringing it to the cross to be killed. Advocates hold that the language of disease, taken too far, can rob a person of the very agency and hope the gospel offers, leaving them a permanent patient managing a chronic condition rather than a sinner being set free by a mighty Savior. They point to the real deliverances Scripture promises, the new heart, the broken chains, the freedom of the sons of God, and they insist that to treat the addict as merely sick is to withhold the strongest medicine there is, repentance and the transforming grace of Christ. They are guarding against a real danger, a therapeutic culture that has so medicalized every human struggle that it has emptied out the categories of sin, responsibility, and repentance, leaving people with explanations for their bondage but no power to be freed from it, managed in their captivity rather than delivered out of it. Against that, they hold the high view of grace, that the gospel does more than help a person cope, it sets the prisoner free, and the wisest among them are careful never to use the language of sin as a club, knowing that the same Jesus who calls sin sin will not break a bruised reed.

views.view: Addiction is a complex bondage of body and soul requiring grace and medicine together
views.body: This view begins with the same conviction that sin is real and that the cross is the deepest answer, and insists that addiction is also a genuine affliction of the body that grace works to heal through medical means, not around them. Advocates hold that to treat addiction as sin alone, addressed by repentance alone, is to ignore the rewired brain, the physical dependence, and the real biology of craving, and that this well-meaning reductionism has driven addicts from churches and sometimes into early graves, told to pray harder while a treatable, deadly condition went untreated. They point to the God who fed Elijah before he preached to him, who made the body and heals it through physicians and medicine, and they insist that the medication, the treatment program, and the recovery community are not rivals to grace but instruments of it. They are guarding against a real danger too, a harsh moralism that loads the suffering addict with shame, that treats relapse as proof of insincere repentance rather than a known feature of a long recovery, and that withholds life-saving treatment in the name of spiritual purity. Against that, they hold that a person is body and soul together and must be healed as both, and the wisest among them are careful never to let the language of disease dissolve the real moral agency and the real hope of deliverance that the gospel holds out to every captive.

parts.title: What Grace Forms on the Road Back
parts.body:
I have to be careful here, because addiction is a bondage and a wreckage, not a gift, and I will not tell you God enslaved you to teach you something. He did not. But the God who meets people at the bottom, in the place where their own strength has finally run out, has a long habit of building things there that the self-sufficient never receive, and naming them is not the same as pretending the bottom was good. The bottom was real. And grace does its deepest work there.

Grace forms, first, the end of the illusion of self-sufficiency, which is the very thing the recovery rooms call the gift of desperation. The addict who has finally admitted he is powerless, who has stopped pretending he can manage this himself, has been brought to the exact place the gospel says every human being must come, the end of self-salvation. This is the hardest gift and the most freeing, because the illusion of self-sufficiency was always the real bondage, the thing standing between a person and the grace that was there all along. Blessed are the poor in spirit, Jesus said, and the addict at the bottom is poor in spirit in a way the comfortable religious person almost never manages to be. The kingdom is nearer to him than he knows.

Grace forms a brutal and liberating honesty. Addiction runs on secrecy and denial, the elaborate lies told to others and the deeper lies told to the self, and recovery begins when the lying stops, when a person says the true thing out loud in a room of people who have said it too. The searching and fearless moral inventory the Steps require is nothing but confession, and the believer who has done it knows a freedom the perpetually polished never taste, the freedom of being fully known and not rejected, of having nothing left to hide. The performance self, so heavy to carry, finally gets set down, and the person discovers they were never loved for the performance anyway.

Grace forms a one-day-at-a-time dependence that is, at bottom, the Christian life itself. The recovering addict learns to live on daily bread, to receive sobriety as a gift each morning rather than an achievement banked, to depend on a power outside himself for the next twenty-four hours, and this is not a lesser spirituality but the real one, stripped of pretense. Give us this day our daily bread is the prayer of someone who has stopped imagining they can stockpile tomorrow's strength, and the addict in recovery prays it with a comprehension the rest of us only theorize about. And grace forms, finally, a tenderness toward other captives that becomes the most useful thing in the church. The recovering addict who has been met by grace becomes the one who can sit with the next person at the bottom and say, without a trace of contempt, I have been where you are, and there is a way out, and you do not walk it alone. The twelfth step is to carry the message, and it is also the great commission, and in the person grace has freed, the two have become the same thing.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Recovery is not admired into existence and it is not won by a single dramatic decision. It is walked, one day at a time, with help, and the road is long and rarely straight. Two things before the list, and they matter more than anything else here. First, if you are in active addiction, you cannot do this alone, and you are not meant to. Reach for professional and medical help now. The SAMHSA National Helpline in the United States is free, confidential, and available around the clock at 1-800-662-4357, and they will help you find treatment. Withdrawal from alcohol and some other substances can be medically dangerous, so do not detox alone, see a doctor. Second, and read this twice. If addiction, shame, or despair has brought you to the edge, if you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the United States, right now, and tell someone who loves you. Your life is not the sum of your worst days. It is a gift God is not finished giving.

steps: Tell one person the truth, the actual truth, about what has hold of you. Addiction lives in secrecy, and saying it out loud to one safe person is the first crack in the wall. A pastor, a friend, a counselor, a helpline. Break the silence this week.

Call the SAMHSA helpline at 1-800-662-4357 or your doctor and ask for help finding treatment. If you are physically dependent on alcohol or other substances, ask specifically about safe, medically supervised detox. Do not try to white-knuckle a dangerous withdrawal alone.

Find one recovery meeting, in person or online, and go this week, before you feel ready, because you will never feel ready. Just go and sit in the back. You do not have to say anything. You only have to be in the room.

Pray the prayer of the powerless, honestly. Not the prayer that promises to do better, which you have prayed and broken many times, but the prayer that admits you cannot do this and asks the One who can. Romans 7 ends in exactly that cry, and so does freedom.

Get into real treatment and stay in it, whatever form fits your situation, outpatient, inpatient, counseling, medication-assisted treatment if it is indicated. Follow the medical advice. Recovery is a course of care, not a single event, and quitting at the first hard week is the most common way it fails.

Keep going to meetings, and get a sponsor or a recovery mentor, someone walking the road ahead of you whom you can call when the craving rises. You cannot do this on willpower and you were never meant to do it alone. The community is not optional. It is the mechanism.

Identify your triggers honestly, the people, places, times, and feelings that precede the craving, and change the architecture of your days to reduce them. This is not weakness. It is wisdom, the same wisdom Proverbs shows when it tells you to keep far from the door of the seductress.

Tell your story to God without hiding any of it. Begin the searching moral inventory that recovery and Scripture both require, not to punish yourself but to be free, bringing the whole truth to the One who already knows it and forgives it.

Build a sober rhythm of life, the boring scaffolding that holds recovery up, regular sleep, regular meals, regular meetings, regular worship, daily prayer. The substance organized your days for a long time, and now something good has to take that place, deliberately, one ordinary day at a time.

Plan for relapse without planning to relapse, by deciding now what you will do if it happens, who you will call, how you will get back into the room the same day. Relapse is a known feature of the long road for many, and it is not the end. It is a setback to walk back from, not a verdict to drown in.

Make amends where you safely can, the way recovery and the gospel both require, repairing what your addiction damaged in the people around you, not to buy back their trust but to live in the truth and let healing begin where it is possible.

Let yourself be carried by grace and community when your own strength is gone, and learn to receive sobriety as a daily gift rather than an achievement you must defend. Give us this day our daily bread is the recovering person's truest prayer.

Stay in recovery for the long haul, because this is not a problem you solve and close but a freedom you keep receiving, one day at a time, for the rest of your life. The people who stay free are almost always the people who never stopped going to the meetings and never stopped depending on grace.

Tend the deeper wounds underneath the addiction, the trauma, the pain, the restless heart, in counseling and in prayer, because the substance was usually a way of medicating something, and lasting freedom reaches all the way down to what you were reaching for it to numb.

Carry the message to the next captive, which is the twelfth step and the great commission at once, becoming for someone else the person who met you with grace and not contempt, who said I have been where you are and there is a way out. The freed become the church's best company for the still-bound.

Keep returning to the One whose grace did what your willpower never could, until your sobriety and your love for the God who freed you have become, in you, the same thing, and you can say with Paul, who could not save himself either, thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord, who delivered me.
